This is NPR News Now. The latest headlines every hour.
Live from NPR News in Culver City, California, I'm Dua Halisa Kautau. The U.S. military says
it has disabled a commercial ship in the Gulf of Amman as it attempted to break the U.S. blockade
of Iranian ports. The strike comes as the Trump administration has been non-committal on its next
moves nine months into the war in Iran. More on this from NPR's Kat Lonsdorf. U.S. Central Command
says a military aircraft fired "precision munitions" at a merchant vessel attempting to leave an Iranian
port. CENTCOM said in a statement that the civilian crew of the ship was unharmed. The U.S. military has
been blocking Iranian ports since April. It temporarily lifted the blockade over the summer
during talks with Tehran but resumed it in July. This strike was the 15th ship the U.S. has disclosed
disabling during its blockade, including at least two strikes that have resulted in the killing of
multiple crew members. President Trump has wavered on what to do next in Iran, suggesting on Thanksgiving
Day that the end of the war will be "whenever he decides." Kat Lonsdorf, NPR News, Washington.
The Norwegian airline North Atlantic has filed for bankruptcy, canceling flights and halting
ticket sales. The airline was unable to resolve financial difficulties caused by soaring fuel
prices, as Esme Nicholson reports. Budget carrier North Atlantic Airways has stopped all flights
and services effective immediately. This impacts a number of long-haul routes from Europe to the U.S.,
Asia, and Africa. Parent company North Atlantic ASA said in a statement that insolvency was
unavoidable despite extensive efforts to find a solution. It also apologized to passengers,
employees and partners. With the most recent barrel prices up 72 percent year-on-year,
the airline could no longer afford jet fuel. Attempts to find short-term financing failed
this week. For NPR News, I'm Esme Nicholson in Berlin. Millions of dollars were spent on
campaign ads generated or enhanced by artificial intelligence this past election cycle. This didn't
appear to affect the outcome of midterm elections, but campaigns are likely to use more of them in
the future, as NPR's Maham Javed reports. At least $187 million was spent during the
midterms on ads that used AI, according to the nonpartisan Wesleyan Media Project. Experts say
the ads didn't connect with many voters in this cycle. But as the technology gets better, the ads
will become more convincing. And it'll be harder to detect what is real, says Brian Riddle, a GOP
strategist. It's not just about convincing some people that fake things are real. Sometimes it's
about people thinking that real things are now fake. Riddle says the AI ads are also cheaper,
making them especially attractive for down-ballot candidates. Maham Javed, NPR News. The S&P 500
index rose 1.6% on Friday. This is NPR News. A report from a criminal justice nonprofit research
group documents hundreds of allegations of abuse inside juvenile detention centers in the U.S.
That's since 2015. The findings come from the sentencing project. NPR's Meg Anderson says the
report cites documents that include audits, inspections, and lawsuits. The abuse described
in the report includes physical violence from both staff and young people, allegations of
sexual abuse, and unsafe conditions like extreme temperatures, among others. Solchil Larios was not
surprised. She's an advocate for incarcerated youth and spent time in juvenile detention herself
when she was a teenager. She says being detained was the opposite of what she needed. When I was
incarcerated, I needed housing. I needed positive relationships. I needed mental health services.
Research shows juvenile detention is damaging to a child's mental health and increases the odds of
recidivism. Advocates say there are better alternatives for nonviolent young offenders.
Meg Anderson, NPR News. Spaniards will head to the polls on Sunday to decide if they want to
keep Pedro Sanchez as prime minister after eight years of leftist leadership or choose Alberto
Nunez-Fejo of the conservative Partido Popular Party moving the country farther to the right.
But there's also the Vox Party led by Santiago Abascal. His group could get enough votes this
time to maybe build a coalition government. The snap election was called after protest and unrest
over housing cost, inflation, and immigration. You're listening to NPR News from Culver City.
